articles.title: Severe bleeding
articles.summary: Blood spurting, pooling or soaking through cloth.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Blood is spurting or flowing steadily.
Blood soaks through cloth quickly or pools on the ground.
The person may become pale, cold, sweaty or confused.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Protect your hands with gloves or a plastic bag if you can, but do not delay.
Press hard and directly on the wound with a clean cloth, or your hand if nothing else is available.
Keep pressing firmly without stopping for at least 10 minutes.
If blood soaks through, put more cloth on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first layer.

sections.title: Then
items: Help the person lie down and keep them warm.
Once bleeding is controlled, tie a bandage firmly over the dressing without cutting off circulation.
Stay with them and watch their breathing until help arrives.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not keep lifting the cloth to check the wound.
Do not pull out objects stuck in the wound. Press around them instead.
Do not give food or drink.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure.
The person becomes pale, cold, clammy, drowsy or confused (signs of shock).
The wound is deep, on the neck, chest or abdomen, or from a high-speed accident.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Tell the 112 operator where you are and how much blood has been lost.
Send someone to meet the ambulance if you can.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that firm pressure cannot control may need a manufactured tourniquet applied by someone trained to use one.
This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020

articles.title: Minor cuts and scrapes
articles.summary: Small wounds that stop bleeding with light pressure.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: A small cut or graze with light bleeding that slows with pressure.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Wash your hands.
Rinse the wound under clean running water.
Press with a clean cloth until bleeding stops.
Cover with a clean dressing or plaster.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep the wound clean and dry and change the dressing daily or when it gets wet or dirty.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not use cotton wool directly on the wound; fibres stick to it.
Do not put home pastes, powders, dung, soil or oil on wounds.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Pain, redness or swelling gets worse, or pus appears.
You develop a fever or feel unwell.
The wound is deep, gaping, or will not stop bleeding.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 if bleeding is heavy and will not stop with firm pressure.
See a doctor or nurse for deep or dirty wounds, animal bites, or if you are unsure your tetanus vaccination is up to date.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Nosebleeds
articles.summary: Bleeding from one or both nostrils.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Blood from one or both nostrils, sometimes running down the throat.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Sit down and lean forward, not back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose, just above the nostrils, firmly.
Keep pinching for 10 to 15 minutes while breathing through the mouth.
Spit out any blood that reaches the mouth.

sections.title: Then
items: If it still bleeds, pinch again for another 10 to 15 minutes.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not tilt the head back or lie down; blood can run into the throat.
Do not pack the nose with cloth or paper.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes or is very heavy.
It started after a head injury.
The person has trouble breathing, feels faint, or takes blood-thinning medicine.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Go to a hospital or call 112 if bleeding will not stop.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Nosebleed

articles.title: Embedded objects
articles.summary: Glass, metal, wood or other objects stuck in a wound.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Something is lodged in the wound and may be holding back bleeding.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Leave the object in place.
Press firmly on either side of the object, not on it, to control bleeding.
Build up padding around the object so it cannot move.
Bandage around the padding without pressing on the object.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep the person still and lying down if they feel faint.
Call 112 for large objects or heavy bleeding.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not pull the object out. It may be plugging the wound.
Do not cut or shorten the object unless rescuers tell you to.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Bleeding is heavy or the object is in the eye, head, chest, neck or abdomen.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Small splinters can be removed with clean tweezers. Anything larger should be removed by a medical professional.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

articles.title: Adult CPR basics
articles.summary: For an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: They do not respond when you shout and tap their shoulders.
They are not breathing, or only gasping. Gasping is not normal breathing.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Ask someone to bring an AED (defibrillator) if one is nearby.
Kneel beside them. Put the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone, and the other hand on top.
Push straight down hard, about 5 to 6 cm, and let the chest come back up fully each time.
Push fast: 100 to 120 times a minute, roughly two per second.
If you are trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. Otherwise keep doing compressions without stopping.

sections.title: Then
items: When the AED arrives, switch it on and follow its voice instructions.
Keep going until help takes over, the AED tells you to stop, or the person starts breathing normally.
If they start breathing normally, put them in the recovery position and keep watching their breathing.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not stop compressions for more than a few seconds.
Do not worry about hurting them. Doing CPR is far better than doing nothing.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Anyone who needs CPR needs emergency care. Always call 112.

sections.title: Getting help
items: The 112 operator can coach you through CPR on the phone.
If you are tired and someone else can help, swap every 2 minutes.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This is for adults. Babies and children need a different technique.
This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Choking
articles.summary: Something blocking the airway of an adult or older child.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: They suddenly cannot speak, breathe or cough, or are clutching their throat.
Their face may turn red, then blue or grey.

sections.title: Do this now
items: If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot cough or breathe, stand to the side and slightly behind them and help them lean forward.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that does not work, stand behind them, put a fist between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, grasp it with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards up to 5 times.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.

sections.title: Then
items: Call 112 if the blockage does not clear.
If they become unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call 112 and start CPR.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not put your fingers blindly into their mouth.
Do not use abdominal thrusts on babies under 1 year.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: They become unresponsive or the blockage does not clear.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor afterwards, even if they feel fine.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: Babies, pregnant women and people who are very obese need different techniques.
This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020

articles.title: Unconsciousness
articles.summary: Someone who does not respond to voice or touch.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: They do not respond when you speak loudly and tap their shoulders.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Check the area is safe for you.
Tilt their head back gently and lift the chin to open the airway.
Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
If they are not breathing normally, call 112 and start CPR.
If they are breathing normally, roll them onto their side into the recovery position and call 112.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep checking their breathing until help arrives.
Keep them warm.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not give anything to eat or drink.
Do not leave them alone if you can avoid it.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Breathing changes or stops: start CPR.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Tell the 112 operator what happened and whether they are breathing.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: If you suspect a neck or back injury, keep the head and neck still and only move them if the airway is at risk.
This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020

articles.title: Shock
articles.summary: Dangerously low blood flow, often after bleeding, burns or severe illness.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Pale, cold and clammy skin.
Fast, weak pulse and fast, shallow breathing.
Dizziness, weakness, confusion or drowsiness.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Treat the cause if you can, for example by pressing on a bleeding wound.
Help them lie down.
Keep them warm with a blanket or clothing, including underneath them if the ground is cold.
Loosen tight clothing.

sections.title: Then
items: Stay with them, reassure them and keep checking their breathing.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not give food or drink.
Do not let them get up or walk around.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Shock is always an emergency. Call 112.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Be ready to start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

references.title: First aid

articles.title: Thermal burns
articles.summary: Burns and scalds from fire, hot liquids, steam or hot surfaces.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Red, painful, blistered, white or charred skin after contact with heat.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Stop the burning: move away from the heat; if clothing is on fire, stop, drop and roll.
Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn, unless it is stuck to the skin.
After cooling, cover the burn loosely with cling film laid in strips, or a clean plastic bag.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep the person warm while you cool the burn.
Raise a burnt arm or leg if you can.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not use ice or iced water.
Do not put butter, ghee, oil, toothpaste or any home paste on the burn.
Do not burst blisters or peel off stuck clothing.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: The burn is larger than the person's hand, deep, white or charred.
It is on the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals, or blisters there.
It is a chemical or electrical burn, or smoke was inhaled.
The person is a child, pregnant, elderly or unwell.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 or go to hospital for any of the signs above.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Burns and scalds
International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

articles.title: Sprains and strains
articles.summary: Twisted or overstretched joints and muscles.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Pain, swelling or bruising around a joint or muscle.
It hurts to move or put weight on it.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Rest it and avoid putting weight on it.
Put an ice pack or cold cloth, wrapped in a towel, on it for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.
Support it with a bandage that is firm but not tight.
Raise it above heart level when you can.

sections.title: Then
items: Gently start moving it after a couple of days as pain allows.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not put ice directly on the skin.
For the first 2 to 3 days, avoid heat, massage, alcohol and running.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: You cannot put any weight on it or use it.
The joint looks misshapen, or there is numbness or the skin turns pale or blue.
Pain is severe or not improving after a few days.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Severe pain or deformity may mean a fracture: see the Suspected fractures guide.
Call 112 if bone is visible, or the limb below is cold, pale or numb.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Sprains and strains

articles.title: Suspected fractures
articles.summary: Possible broken bones.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Severe pain, swelling, bruising or a limb at an odd angle.
The person cannot use the limb, or bone is visible through the skin.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Keep the person and the injured part still, in the position you found it.
Support the injury with padding such as rolled clothing.
If there is a wound, cover it with a clean dressing and press around, not on, any bone.
Call 112 for injuries to the leg, hip, pelvis, neck or back, or where bone shows.

sections.title: Then
items: Watch for signs of shock and keep them warm.
A cold pack wrapped in cloth can ease swelling.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not try to straighten the limb.
Do not move someone with a possible neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
Do not give food or drink; they may need surgery.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: The skin below the injury is cold, pale or numb.
There are signs of shock, or the injury is to the head, neck, back or thigh.

sections.title: Getting help
items: If you must move the person, only splint the limb if you know how.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

references.title: First aid

articles.title: Head injuries
articles.summary: Bumps and blows to the head.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: A blow to the head followed by headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion.

sections.title: Do this now
items: If they are unresponsive, call 112 and follow the Unconsciousness guide.
Keep the head and neck still if a neck injury is possible.
For a minor bump, hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on it.
Rest and avoid strenuous activity.

sections.title: Then
items: Have someone stay with them for the first 24 hours.
Watch for any of the urgent signs below.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not leave them alone for the first day.
Do not drink alcohol or take sleeping tablets afterwards.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: They were knocked out, even briefly, or have a seizure.
Repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion or unusual drowsiness.
Problems speaking, seeing, walking or understanding.
Clear fluid or blood from the ears or nose, or bruising behind the ears.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 or go to hospital for any of these signs.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Head injury and concussion

articles.title: Eye injuries
articles.summary: Chemicals, objects or blows to the eye.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Pain, redness, watering or blurred vision after something entered or struck the eye.

sections.title: Do this now
items: For chemicals: rinse the eye straight away with lots of clean running water for at least 15 to 20 minutes, holding the eyelids open.
Remove contact lenses if they come out easily.
For dust or grit: blink and rinse with clean water.
For an object stuck in the eye: cover the eye without pressing on it, for example with a paper cup.

sections.title: Then
items: Get urgent medical help for chemical splashes and objects stuck in the eye.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not rub the eye.
Do not try to remove an object stuck in the eye.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Any chemical splash, embedded object, cut to the eye or loss of vision.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 for serious chemical splashes or sudden loss of vision.
Take the chemical container or its name with you to hospital.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

articles.title: Electrical injuries
articles.summary: Electric shock from appliances, wiring or power lines.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Contact with electricity, burns at entry and exit points, unresponsiveness.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Do not touch the person until the power is off. Switch off at the mains or unplug.
For power lines or high-voltage equipment, stay well away and call 112 and the electricity provider.
Once safe, check breathing. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR.
Cool any burns under cool running water.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep them still and warm until help arrives.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not touch them with your bare hands while they are in contact with the source.
Do not go near fallen power lines.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Everyone who has had a significant electric shock needs medical assessment, even if they seem fine.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

articles.title: Heatstroke
articles.summary: A life-threatening rise in body temperature.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Very high body temperature and hot skin, which may be dry or sweaty.
Confusion, slurred speech, fits, or collapse.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Move them to a cool, shaded place.
Remove extra clothing.
Cool them as fast as you can: wet the skin with cool water and fan them, and put cold packs or cold wet cloths on the neck, armpits and groin.
If they are alert and can swallow, give small sips of cool water.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep cooling until help arrives.
If they become unresponsive but are breathing, put them in the recovery position.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not give medicines for fever; they do not treat heatstroke.
Do not give drinks to someone who is confused or unresponsive.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Heatstroke is always an emergency. Call 112.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Follow the Heat exhaustion guide for milder symptoms.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
National Action Plan on Heat Related Illnesses
references.publisher: National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India

articles.title: Heat exhaustion
articles.summary: Overheating and fluid loss that can lead to heatstroke.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps, tiredness and fast pulse.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Move them to a cool place and help them lie down with their feet slightly raised.
Give plenty of water or oral rehydration solution.
Cool their skin with a spray or wet cloth and fan them.
Put cold packs wrapped in cloth on the armpits or neck.

sections.title: Then
items: They should start to feel better within 30 minutes.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not give alcohol or caffeinated drinks.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: No improvement after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids.
Confusion, fits, very high temperature or collapse: treat as heatstroke and call 112.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Children, older people and people with long-term illness can get worse quickly.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
National Action Plan on Heat Related Illnesses
references.publisher: National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India

articles.title: Hypothermia
articles.summary: Dangerously low body temperature.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Shivering, pale and cold skin, slurred speech, slow breathing, tiredness and confusion.
In severe cases shivering stops and they become drowsy.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Move them somewhere warm and out of the wind.
Remove wet clothing.
Wrap them in dry blankets or clothes, including the head, and insulate them from the ground.
If they are alert, give warm, sweet, non-alcoholic drinks.

sections.title: Then
items: Warm them gradually. Sharing body heat under blankets can help.
Handle them gently.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not put them in a hot bath.
Do not rub their arms and legs or put hot water bottles or heaters directly on the skin.
Do not give alcohol.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: They stop shivering, become drowsy or confused, or breathe slowly: call 112.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Keep checking breathing. Start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Hypothermia

articles.title: Dehydration
articles.summary: Losing more fluid than you take in.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Thirst, dark yellow urine, peeing less, dry mouth, tiredness and dizziness.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Drink fluids regularly in small amounts.
For diarrhoea or vomiting, use oral rehydration salts (ORS) mixed exactly as the packet says.
If vomiting, take small sips every few minutes.
Rest in a cool place.

sections.title: Then
items: Keep drinking until urine is pale and normal in amount.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not mix ORS with more or less water than the packet says.
Do not rely on sugary soft drinks or alcohol.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Confusion, fainting, a fast heartbeat or no urine for 8 hours or more.
Sunken eyes, or a sunken soft spot on a baby's head.
Diarrhoea or vomiting that will not stop, or blood in it.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 if the person is confused, faints or is very drowsy.
Babies, young children and older people need medical advice sooner.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Dehydration
Oral rehydration salts

articles.title: Severe allergic reactions
articles.summary: Anaphylaxis: a life-threatening allergic reaction.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Swelling of the throat, tongue or face, or difficulty breathing or wheezing.
Feeling faint, clammy skin, a fast heartbeat, confusion or collapse.
Often after a sting, food or medicine, and sometimes with a rash.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
If they have an adrenaline auto-injector, help them use it in the outer thigh, following the device instructions.
Lie them down with their legs raised. If breathing is difficult, let them sit up.
Remove the trigger if you can, for example scrape away a sting.

sections.title: Then
items: If there is no improvement after 5 minutes and a second auto-injector is available, use it.
Start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not let them stand up or walk, even if they feel better.
Do not wait to see if symptoms improve before calling 112.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Anaphylaxis is always an emergency, even if symptoms ease.

sections.title: Getting help
items: They must go to hospital after using an auto-injector.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: Only use an auto-injector prescribed for that person, as instructed on it.
This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Anaphylaxis

references.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

articles.title: Insect stings
articles.summary: Bee, wasp and other insect stings.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Pain, redness and swelling at the sting.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Scrape out a sting left in the skin sideways with a fingernail or card edge.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Hold a cold pack or cold wet cloth on it for at least 10 minutes.
Raise the area if you can.

sections.title: Then
items: Watch closely for signs of a severe allergic reaction.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not squeeze the sting.
Do not scratch the area.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Any signs of anaphylaxis: call 112.
Many stings, or stings in the mouth or throat.
Scorpion stings in children, or severe pain, sweating or vomiting after any sting.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Seek medical advice if swelling keeps spreading after a day or two.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Insect bites and stings

articles.title: Animal bites
articles.summary: Bites and scratches from dogs, monkeys, cats, bats and other mammals.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: A bite, scratch or lick on broken skin from an animal.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Wash the wound straight away with soap and plenty of running water for about 15 minutes.
Apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine if you have it.
Cover it with a clean dressing.
Go to a hospital or health centre the same day.

sections.title: Then
items: Tell the doctor which animal it was. You may need rabies vaccine and other treatment.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not wait to see whether the animal becomes ill before getting care.
Do not apply chilli, oil, lime or home pastes to the wound.
Do not close the wound with tape or stitches yourself.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: The wound bleeds heavily, is on the face, head, neck or hands, or is deep.
Signs of infection: increasing pain, redness, swelling or fever.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 for heavy bleeding or deep bites to the face or neck.
Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, but treatment after a bite prevents it. Do not delay.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Rabies fact sheet
Animal and human bites

articles.title: Snakebite
articles.summary: Bites from snakes, which may be venomous.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Fang marks, pain or swelling; sometimes none at first.
Later: drowsiness, drooping eyelids, difficulty breathing, bleeding, or vomiting.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Move away from the snake.
Keep the person calm and as still as possible.
Keep the bitten limb still, for example with a splint or sling.
Remove rings, bangles, anklets and tight clothing near the bite.
Get them to hospital quickly, carrying them if possible.

sections.title: Then
items: Note the time of the bite. Antivenom is given in hospital.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not cut, suck or burn the wound.
Do not tie a tourniquet or tight cord.
Do not apply ice, herbs or chemicals, and do not wait for a traditional healer.
Do not try to catch or kill the snake.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Every snakebite should be treated as an emergency, even if the person feels fine.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Tell the hospital what the snake looked like only if it was seen safely.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

references.title: Snakebite envenoming fact sheet

articles.title: Suspected poisoning
articles.summary: Swallowing, breathing in or touching something harmful.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Vomiting, drowsiness, burns around the mouth, unusual smell on the breath, or an empty container nearby.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Find out what was taken, how much and when. Keep the container or packet.
If they are unresponsive but breathing, put them in the recovery position.
If they are not breathing normally, start CPR, using a face shield if you have one.
For chemicals on the skin, remove contaminated clothing and rinse the skin with running water for 20 minutes.

sections.title: Then
items: For fumes or gas, move them into fresh air only if it is safe for you.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not make them vomit.
Do not give anything to eat or drink unless a medical professional tells you to.
Do not give salt water, oil or milk as remedies.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: All suspected poisonings need medical help, including pesticides and household chemicals.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Take the container, packet or a photo of the label to the hospital.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Seizures
articles.summary: Fits, with jerking movements or loss of awareness.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Sudden stiffening and jerking, loss of awareness, sometimes biting the tongue or losing bladder control.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Stay calm and note the time it started.
Move hard or sharp objects away, and cushion their head.
Loosen anything tight around the neck.
When the jerking stops, roll them onto their side into the recovery position.

sections.title: Then
items: Stay with them, speak calmly and let them rest until fully alert.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not hold them down or try to stop the movements.
Do not put anything in their mouth.
Do not hold shoes, onions or anything else to their nose.
Do not give food or drink until they are fully alert.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: It is their first seizure, or it lasts more than 5 minutes.
They have another seizure without waking in between.
They are injured, have trouble breathing, or it happened in water.
They are pregnant or have diabetes.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 for any of the signs above.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Fainting
articles.summary: A brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Feeling light-headed, sweaty or sick, then briefly losing consciousness.

sections.title: Do this now
items: If someone feels faint, help them lie down or sit with the head between the knees.
If they faint, lay them on their back and raise their legs, for example on a bag or chair.
Check they are breathing.
When they come round, let them sit up slowly.

sections.title: Then
items: Give water once they are fully alert.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not let them stand up quickly.
Do not crowd them; give them air.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: They do not wake up within 1 to 2 minutes.
Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or difficulty breathing.
They hit their head, or have trouble speaking, seeing or moving.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Call 112 for any of the signs above.
Anyone who faints for no clear reason should see a doctor.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Chest pain
articles.summary: Possible heart attack.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Pressure, tightness or pain in the chest that may spread to the arms, neck, jaw, back or stomach.
Shortness of breath, sweating, nausea or light-headedness.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Help them sit down and rest in a comfortable position, often half-sitting.
Loosen tight clothing.
If they have their own prescribed chest-pain medicine, help them take it as prescribed.

sections.title: Then
items: The 112 operator may advise them to chew an aspirin if they are not allergic. Follow their advice.
Be ready to start CPR if they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not let them walk around or drive themselves to hospital.
Do not wait to see if the pain goes away.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Chest pain lasting more than a few minutes is an emergency.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Note when the pain started; tell the paramedics.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.

articles.title: Stroke
articles.summary: Sudden loss of blood supply to part of the brain.

sections.title: Recognise it
items: Face: one side droops or they cannot smile evenly.
Arms: they cannot lift both arms and keep them up.
Speech: slurred, confused or unable to speak.
Time: if you see any of these, it is time to call 112.

sections.title: Do this now
items: Call 112. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep helping.
Note the time symptoms started.
Keep them comfortable and reassure them.
If they become unresponsive but are breathing, put them in the recovery position.

sections.title: Then
items: Stay with them until help arrives.

sections.title: Do not
items: Do not give food, drink or medicine; swallowing may be affected.
Do not wait to see if symptoms pass.

sections.title: Get urgent help if
items: Any sign of stroke, even if it goes away, needs emergency care.

sections.title: Getting help
items: Treatment works best when started early, so the start time matters.

sections.title: Limits of this guide
items: This guide does not replace training. A certified first-aid course is the best preparation.
